modules.title: Standard phrases & conventions
modules.summary: Phonetic alphabet with exact CASA pronunciations, number transmission rules, and the full standard phrases table (CASA Table 21). The foundations every transmission relies on.

content.text: CASA's Radiotelephony Manual (Multi-Part AC 64.B-02 / AC 91-35 / AC 172-05, Dec 2025) is the authoritative source for the phrases below. The exact pronunciations matter under formal IPC standards — 'FIFE' for five and 'NIN-er' for nine are CASA-prescribed, not stylistic.

items: A ALFA (AL-fah) · B BRAVO (BRAH-voh) · C CHARLIE (CHAR-lee or SHAR-lee) · D DELTA (DELL-tah) · E ECHO (ECK-oh)
F FOXTROT (FOKS-trot) · G GOLF (GOLF) · H HOTEL (ho-TELL) · I INDIA (IN-dee-ah) · J JULIETT (JEW-lee-ETT)
K KILO (KEY-loh) · L LIMA (LEE-mah) · M MIKE (MIKE) · N NOVEMBER (no-VEM-ber) · O OSCAR (OSS-cah)
P PAPA (pah-PAH) · Q QUEBEC (keh-BECK) · R ROMEO (ROW-me-oh) · S SIERRA (see-AIR-rah) · T TANGO (TANG-go)
U UNIFORM (YOU-nee-form or OO-nee-form) · V VICTOR (VIK-tah) · W WHISKEY (WISS-key)
X X-RAY (ECKS-ray) · Y YANKEE (YANG-key) · Z ZULU (ZOO-loo)
0 ZE-RO · 1 WUN · 2 TOO · 3 TREE · 4 FOW-er · 5 FIFE · 6 SIX · 7 SEV-en · 8 AIT · 9 NIN-er
Decimal: DAY-SEE-MAL — used in 'one two one DAY-SEE-MAL seven' for 121.7.
Hundred: HUN-dred · Thousand: TOU-SAND.

content.text: When to use digits vs whole numbers

items: Default — pronounce each digit separately. Callsigns, headings, runways, frequencies, squawks, RVR, visibility all use digits.
Flight levels with WHOLE HUNDREDS may be said as 'two hundred' for FL200; otherwise digit-by-digit ('one eight zero' for FL180).
Altitudes with whole hundreds and thousands use 'HUNDRED' / 'THOUSAND'. 4,500 ft = 'four thousand five hundred'.
Word 'feet' is normally omitted; include it to prevent confusion.
Headings: degrees magnetic, three digits, 'DEGREE' may be omitted. '080' = 'heading zero eight zero'.
Runway designators: 'runway WUN NIN-er' for 19, 'runway ZE RO SIX' for 06, plus L/R/C suffix when applicable.
Time: each digit separately. 0345Z = 'zero three four five'. In position reports, often shortened to minutes only ('at four five').
ACKNOWLEDGE — 'let me know that you have received and understood this message.'
AFFIRM — 'yes.' (Not 'affirmative' — CASA prescribes AFFIRM.)
APPROVED — 'permission for proposed action granted.'
BREAK — separation between portions of one message.
BREAK BREAK — separation between messages to different aircraft in a busy environment.
CANCEL — 'annul the previously transmitted clearance.'
CHECK — 'examine a system or procedure.' No answer expected.
CLEARED — 'authorised to proceed under the conditions specified.'
CONFIRM — 'I request verification of: (clearance, instruction, action, information).'
CONTACT — 'establish communications with …'
CORRECT — 'true or accurate.'
CORRECTION — 'an error has been made in this transmission, the correct version is …'
DISREGARD — 'ignore.'
HOW DO YOU READ? — 'what is the readability of my transmission?' (See §2.17 in the AC for full radio-check phraseology.)
I SAY AGAIN — 'I repeat for clarity or emphasis.'
MAINTAIN — 'continue in accordance with the condition(s) specified' (or literal — 'maintain VFR').
MONITOR — 'listen out on (frequency).'
NEGATIVE — 'no / permission not granted / that is not correct / not capable.'
OUT — 'my transmission is ended and I expect no response.' Not normally used on VHF.
OVER — 'my transmission is ended and I expect a response.' Not normally used on VHF or satellite.
READ BACK — 'repeat all, or the specified part, of this message back to me exactly as received.'
RECLEARED — 'a change has been made to your last clearance and this new clearance supersedes your previous clearance.'
REPORT — 'pass me the following information.'
REQUEST — 'I should like to know / I wish to obtain.'
ROGER — 'I have received all of your last transmission.' Never used in reply to a question requiring a read back or a yes/no answer.
SAY AGAIN — 'repeat all, or the following part, of your last transmission.'
SPEAK SLOWER — 'reduce your rate of speech.'
STANDBY — 'wait and I will call you.'
UNABLE — 'I cannot comply with your request, instruction or clearance' (normally followed by a reason).
VERIFY — 'check and confirm with originator.'
WILCO — 'I understand your message and will comply with it.'
WORDS TWICE — as request: 'communication is difficult, please send every word or group twice.' As info: 'since communication is difficult every word or group will be sent twice.'
Listen out before transmitting — make sure the frequency is clear.
Plan the message before keying — say what's needed, no more.
Speak clearly, evenly, at moderate pace. Higher pitch is more readable than lower.
Avoid courtesies ('please', 'thank you'). CASA AC §2.8.3 explicitly says don't use them — they cost airtime.
'IMMEDIATELY' is reserved for actions required for SAFETY (CASA AC §2.8.4). Don't say it casually.

content: Wilco is NOT a substitute for a mandatory readback. Saying 'Wilco' to a level change is incorrect — that needs a verbatim readback (see RADIO-002).
'Roger' alone is not a frequency-change readback. CASA AC §4.1.2(f) lists frequency instructions as mandatory readback.
Never use 'over' and 'out' together — they're mutually exclusive. On VHF both are normally omitted.
Read digit-by-digit. 'Twelve thousand' is acceptable for altitude; 'twelve hundred' for squawk 1200 is NOT — it's 'one two zero zero'.
'Affirmative' is not CASA standard — say AFFIRM. Old habit dies hard from older RT training.
ATC: 'Mike X-ray Golf, resume own navigation.' — You can comply: 'Wilco, Mike X-ray Golf.' Resume own nav is not a mandatory readback item, so Wilco is correct.
ATC: 'Mike X-ray Golf, climb to flight level two two zero.' — Mandatory readback per CASA AC §4.1.2(e). NOT Wilco. Correct: 'Climb to flight level two two zero, Mike X-ray Golf.'
ATC: 'Mike X-ray Golf, *static* descend *static* zero.' — Garbled. 'Say again your last, Mike X-ray Golf.' (Don't say 'repeat' — that's military.)

modules.title: Mandatory readback items
modules.summary: The CASR Part 91 MOS §11.12 list of clearances and instructions you MUST read back verbatim — recited verbatim in CASA AC §4.1.2. Every readback drill in the library comes from this list.

content.text: CASR Part 91 Manual of Standards §11.12 requires pilots to read back the safety-related parts of any ATC clearance or instruction. CASA's Radiotelephony Manual (Multi-Part AC 91-35) §4.1.2 spells out the six categories below. Read back too little and ATC has no confirmation you copied; read back too much (e.g. wind, traffic info) and you waste frequency time. Memorise the six.

items: ATC route clearances, including any amendments. (Route clearances include departure, en-route, arrival, and approach clearances.)
En-route holding instructions.
Route and runway-holding positions specified in a taxi clearance.
Clearances, conditional clearances, and instructions to taxi on, enter, line up on, wait on, land on, take off from, hold short of, cross, or backtrack on any runway.
Assigned runway or HLS (helicopter landing site), altimeter settings, Mode A transponder codes, data link logon addresses, altitude instructions, heading instructions, and speed instructions.
Radio frequency instructions.

content.text: Don't read back (acknowledge with callsign only)

items: Wind, weather, traffic information — callsign only.
ATIS code (already confirmed on initial contact).
Radar identification ('identified', 'radar contact').
Per CASA AC §4.1.3-4.1.4: instructions that don't require specific read back may be acknowledged with WILCO or ROGER — provided it's clear the instruction is understood and accepted.

content.text: Australian convention — callsign at the END

Australian readbacks finish with the callsign, not start with it. 'Climb to seven thousand, Lima Echo Foxtrot' — not 'Lima Echo Foxtrot, climbing seven thousand'. Initial calls and broadcasts put the addressed station first, then callsign; readbacks reverse this. The CASA AC examples (e.g. Figure 35) show this pattern consistently.
If your readback is wrong, ATC will say 'NEGATIVE' followed by the correct version (CASA AC §4.1.8). On hearing NEGATIVE, re-read the corrected version verbatim — don't argue, don't ask why.

content: Forgetting the callsign on a readback. ATC needs to know it was YOU that copied. No callsign = no readback under CASA AC §4.1.6.
Reading back 'QNH 1008' as 'QNH one thousand eight'. Digit-by-digit: 'one zero zero eight'.
Skipping the turn direction on a heading. 'Heading two seven zero' is incomplete — include 'left' or 'right' so ATC knows which way you'll roll.
Missing the runway operations in category 4 — 'cross runway', 'backtrack runway' are full readback items, not casual acknowledgements.
Reading back data link logon addresses as 'noted'. CASA AC §4.1.2(e) lists them as mandatory readback — say the full address.
Saying just 'roger' to a frequency change. Frequency is mandatory readback per §4.1.2(f).
ATC: 'JRG, QNH 1003.' Pilot: 'QNH one zero zero three, JRG.' (Altimeter setting — §4.1.2(e).)
ATC: 'PQR, contact Ground 121.9.' Pilot: 'Ground one two one decimal nine, PQR.' (Frequency — §4.1.2(f).)
ATC: 'JABIRU 1346, report passing one thousand five hundred.' Pilot: 'Wilco, JABIRU 1346.' (Reporting instruction doesn't require verbatim readback — WILCO suffices per §4.1.4.)

ATC: 'JRG, cleared to GASTOWN via BAVEM, flight planned route, four thousand five hundred, squawk four three three zero.' Pilot: 'GASTOWN via BAVEM, flight planned route, four thousand five hundred, squawk four three three zero, JRG.' (Full route clearance — §4.1.2(a).)

modules.title: Pre-departure & taxi
modules.summary: ATIS request, IFR clearance, SID readback, taxi, line-up, and takeoff clearance. The first half-dozen calls of every controlled-airspace IFR flight.

content.text: These six calls follow the same AIP GEN 3.4 initial-call format: addressed station, callsign, request type with details, ATIS code. Master the rhythm and the rest is variations on the theme.

content: Format: '[Station] Information, [callsign], request aerodrome information.'
Example: 'Bankstown Information, Lima Echo Foxtrot, request aerodrome information.'
Format: '[Tower / Delivery], [callsign], IFR clearance to [destination], information [ATIS code].'
Example: 'Sydney Delivery, Mike X-ray Golf, IFR clearance to Coffs Harbour, information Charlie.'
At smaller Class D fields without a separate Delivery, address Tower or Ground (slot fallback chain in practice).
Format: 'Cleared to [destination] via [route or SID], [level/climb constraint], squawk [code], [callsign].'
Example without SID: 'Cleared to Coffs Harbour via flight planned route, climb to seven thousand, squawk four one two three, Lima Echo Foxtrot.'
Example with SID: 'Cleared to Coffs Harbour via RIVET TWO departure, climb via SID to flight level one eight zero, squawk five six four three, Mike X-ray Golf.'
Format: '[Ground], [callsign], ready for taxi, information [ATIS code].'
Example: 'Sydney Ground, Mike X-ray Golf, ready for taxi, information Charlie.'
Format: '[Tower], [callsign], holding point runway [X], ready.'
Example: 'Bankstown Tower, Lima Echo Foxtrot, holding point runway two nine right, ready.'
Note: you announce readiness — Tower decides when. Don't say 'request take-off'.
Format: 'Cleared for take-off runway [X], [callsign].'
Example: 'Cleared for take-off runway two nine right, Lima Echo Foxtrot.'
Wind, traffic info — acknowledged but NOT read back.
Reading back 'cleared for take-off, wind two eight zero at ten' — drop the wind. Wind is not a readback item.
Saying 'I am ready' instead of 'ready' on the line-up call — extra words, no value.
Reading back a SID by just the name — include 'via [SID name] departure' so ATC knows you have the right one.
Confusing 'climb via SID' with a level instruction. 'Climb via SID' means follow all level constraints on the SID procedure chart — readback the phrase verbatim.

Cold start at Bankstown to Coffs Harbour. ATIS Mike current. Switch through: ATIS confirmation (covered by reading the broadcast) → Tower clearance request → clearance readback → Ground taxi request → taxi readback (route) → Tower ready call → takeoff clearance readback. Six transmissions, all in the GEN 3.4 format.

modules.title: Climb, en-route, & handoffs
modules.summary: Initial Centre check-in, frequency change acks, level / speed readbacks, position reports, direct routing, QNH on descent, and SARTIME — the en-route and transition phase.

content: Format: '[Station], [callsign], [current state + level], [cleared level if climbing/descending].'
Climbing: 'Brisbane Centre, Mike X-ray Golf, climbing flight level one eight zero for flight level two two zero.'
Descending: 'Canberra Approach, Mike X-ray Golf, descending flight level one five zero for nine thousand, information Charlie.'
Centre needs your current state + level to sequence. Always include both 'current' and 'for' (the target level) when not in cruise.
Format: '[New station] [frequency], [callsign].'
Example: 'Sydney Centre one three four decimal eight five, Mike X-ray Golf.'
'Decimal', not 'point'. Read the full frequency digit-by-digit. 'Roger' alone is not a frequency readback.
Climb: 'Climb to flight level two two zero, [callsign].'
Descend: 'Descend to seven thousand, [callsign].'
Heading: '[Left/right] heading two seven zero, [callsign].' Include direction.
Speed: 'Reduce speed to two two zero knots, [callsign].'
Full (initial entry to non-radar area, or as requested): '[Callsign], [waypoint] at [time minutes], flight level [X], [next waypoint] at [ETA minutes].'
Example: 'Mike X-ray Golf, MARLE at four five, flight level two two zero, WALSH at zero eight.'
Abbreviated (when next-waypoint ETA waived): drop the next/ETA section. 'Mike X-ray Golf, MARLE at four five, flight level two two zero.'
Direct: '[Centre], [callsign], request direct [waypoint].'
Descent: '[Centre], [callsign], request descent.'
Both keep it short — let Centre come back with the answer.
Format: 'QNH [value digit-by-digit], [callsign].'
Example: 'QNH one zero zero eight, Mike X-ray Golf.'

Transition altitude in Australia is 10,000 ft — above, you use 1013.2 hPa standard and report flight levels; below, you use local QNH and report altitudes. Set the new QNH BEFORE descending through 10,000 ft.
Submit: '[Centre], [callsign], submit SARTIME [time UTC, digit-by-digit].'
Cancel: '[Centre], [callsign], cancel SARTIME.'
Cancel BEFORE shutting down — un-cancelled SARTIMEs trigger unnecessary SAR mobilisation.
Saying 'point' instead of 'decimal' in a frequency. AIP standard is 'decimal'.
Forgetting to set 1013 above 10,000 ft — a chronic source of altimetry errors and altitude busts.
Reading back a heading without the turn direction. Always include 'left' or 'right'.
Treating Position Report 'time' as the hour. Time in a position report is the MINUTES only (the hour is unambiguous in context). 0345Z reported as 'at four five'.

modules.title: Arrival & approach
modules.summary: Initial Approach contact, descent readback, vectoring, holding instructions, approach clearance, established reports, and visual approach request.

content: Format: '[Approach], [callsign], descending [current level] for [cleared level], information [ATIS code].'
Confirm ATIS up front so Approach doesn't have to ask.
Format: '[Left/right] heading [X], descend to [Y], [callsign].'
Always include the turn direction with the heading — both are mandatory readback items per MATS Part 4.
Full readback: '[Hold at fix] inbound [track], [turn direction if non-standard], maintain [level], expect further clearance at [time], [callsign].'
Example: 'Hold at SMOKO inbound three five zero, right turns, maintain flight level one one zero, expect further clearance at zero five, Mike X-ray Golf.'
EFC time is your lost-comms timer — read it back and write it down.
Format: 'Cleared [approach type] runway [X], [reporting instructions], [callsign].'
Example: 'Cleared ILS runway three five approach, report established, Mike X-ray Golf.'
Read back any reporting instruction ('report established', 'report visual') — it's a MATS readback item.
Format: '[Callsign], established [approach] runway [X].'
Example: 'Mike X-ray Golf, established ILS runway three five.'
Short and specific. No need to repeat the cleared level or other clearance items.
Format: '[Approach], [callsign], airfield in sight, request visual approach runway [X].'
Prerequisite: you must actually see the field. Visual ≠ VFR — still IFR plan, just not flying the published procedure.
Reporting 'established' without naming the approach. Be specific — 'established ILS runway three five', not just 'established'.
Forgetting EFC time on a hold readback. EFC is what you use if comms fail — read it back even if it feels redundant.
Confusing 'request visual' with 'cancel IFR'. They are different — visual keeps you on the IFR plan; cancel IFR terminates IFR service and SAR.

modules.title: Final, missed approach, & post-landing
modules.summary: Landing clearance readback, going around (controlled), missed-approach instruction readback, vacate runway, and the Ground frequency switch.

content: Format: 'Cleared to land runway [X], [callsign].'
Example: 'Cleared to land runway three five, Mike X-ray Golf.'
Drop the wind — not a readback item. Read back 'cleared to land' verbatim (not 'landing').
Format: 'Going around, [callsign].'
Two words plus callsign. Don't try to describe the manoeuvre — Tower is expecting it as a possibility and needs to issue follow-up instructions immediately.
Tower will issue a stack of instructions — heading, climb, and a new frequency. Read them back in the order issued.
Example: 'Runway heading, climb to four thousand, Canberra Approach one two five decimal one, Mike X-ray Golf.'
Format: 'Vacate [direction] via [taxiway], [new freq if issued], [callsign].'
Example: 'Vacate next right via Bravo, Ground one two one decimal nine, Mike X-ray Golf.'
The frequency change is a mandatory readback. The vacate routing isn't strictly mandatory but reading it back confirms for Tower.
Saying 'missed approach' on its own when committing. The standard immediate call is 'going around'. 'Missed approach' is fine as a descriptor but not the recognised announcement.
Reading back landing clearance as 'landing runway three five'. The phrase is 'cleared to land' — verbatim.
Switching to Ground before Tower instructs. Stay on Tower until the explicit handoff.

ILS RWY 35 at Canberra: at the minima you can't acquire the runway environment. Commit: 'Going around, Mike X-ray Golf.' Tower responds with heading + climb + frequency. Read it back as one composite transmission. Switch frequency. New initial contact with Approach announcing the missed approach.

modules.title: CTAF broadcasts (non-towered)
modules.summary: Class G non-towered aerodromes — broadcasts to other pilots, no ATC. Different format, different rules of the air. Knows the calls cold and you fly safer at CTAFs.

content.text: At a CTAF you are talking to OTHER PILOTS, not a controller. There is no sequencing service; the broadcasts are the only thing keeping a runway conflict from becoming a collision. Mandatory broadcast situations at a CTAF are listed below — make them all even if you don't hear anyone reply.

content: Open with: '[Aerodrome] traffic' — addresses everyone on the frequency.
Close with: '[Aerodrome]' — confirms which CTAF you were transmitting on (CTAFs share frequencies regionally).
Full structure: '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], [aircraft type if first call], [position / action / intentions], [Aerodrome].'

items: Taxiing — '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], [type], taxiing for runway [X], [IFR/VFR/circuits], [Aerodrome].'
Departing (rolling) — '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], departing runway [X], [direction], [Aerodrome].'
Inbound at 10 NM (or earlier if airspace) — '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], [type], [distance + bearing], [altitude], inbound for landing runway [X], [Aerodrome].'
Joining circuit — overhead, straight-in, or base join. Each has its own call (see below).
Downwind, base, final — for following traffic spacing.
Clear of runway — releases the runway to following traffic since nobody is watching.
Going around at CTAF — broadcast form (different from controlled).
Crossing a runway while taxiing — warns traffic lined up or on final.
Overflying within 10 NM and below 5000 ft AGL — say 'transiting' so circuit traffic doesn't try to sequence you.

content: Overhead join: '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], overhead the field two thousand five hundred, descending dead side for runway [X], [Aerodrome].'
Straight-in: '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], five miles final runway [X], straight-in approach, [Aerodrome].' CASR Part 91 right-of-way: circuit traffic gives way to straight-in.
Base join: '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], joining base runway [X], [Aerodrome].'
Format: '[Aerodrome] traffic, [callsign], going around runway [X], climbing upwind, [Aerodrome].'
At controlled fields it's just 'going around'. At CTAF you include the runway so other traffic knows which one you're NOT landing on.
Ending with the callsign instead of the aerodrome name. CTAF format ends with the aerodrome. This catches everyone who is used to controlled airspace.
Not making the broadcast because 'no one will hear'. Multiple aerodromes share CTAF frequencies regionally — your traffic might be 30 NM away on the same freq.
Reading back instructions to nobody. At CTAF there is no ATC — broadcasts are statements, not readbacks.
Forgetting the aerodrome name on EVERY broadcast (not just the first). It's the only way other pilots know which CTAF you mean.

Inbound to Mudgee from the south, IFR cancelled at 20 DME. At 10 DME, broadcast: 'Mudgee traffic, Lima Echo Foxtrot, PA-31, ten miles south, four thousand five hundred, inbound for landing runway two two, Mudgee.' Continue with joining circuit call (overhead or base depending on procedure), then downwind, base, final, and clear-of-runway after touchdown.

modules.title: Distress, urgency, & lost comms
modules.summary: MAYDAY format, PAN-PAN format, cancellation, TCAS RA call, and the NORDO / squawk 7600 / blind transmission procedure. Calls you rarely make but must get right cold.

content.text: Distress and urgency calls under AIP GEN 3.6 are formula-driven. Memorise the format and the three-time repetition — under stress, falling back on a memorised pattern is what gets these calls right.

content: Use when: there's a threat to the aircraft or souls on board requiring immediate assistance (engine fire, structural failure, medical, fuel emergency).
Format: 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, [station], [callsign], [nature of distress], [intentions], [souls on board], [fuel remaining].'
Example: 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, Brisbane Centre, Mike X-ray Golf, engine fire left engine, descending, request immediate diversion nearest suitable airport, four souls on board, one hour fuel.'
MAYDAY × 3 is mandatory — it's what gives the call absolute priority on the frequency.
Use when: there's a concern requiring priority handling but NOT immediate threat to life (oil pressure indication, partial loss of one engine still controllable, ill passenger).
Format: 'PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, [station], [callsign], [nature], [intentions], [souls], [fuel].'
Example: 'PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, Brisbane Centre, Mike X-ray Golf, oil pressure failure left engine, requesting descent and diversion to Coffs Harbour, four souls on board, two hours fuel.'
PAN-PAN × 3 — same priority rule as MAYDAY but one rung lower.
Format: '[Station], [callsign], cancel [PAN PAN / MAYDAY], situation resolved.'
Use explicit cancel phrase so the frequency returns to normal and SAR doesn't mobilise unnecessarily.
Format: 'TCAS RA, [callsign].'
Three words. Don't describe the manoeuvre — ATC's job is to clear traffic, not co-pilot the RA.
Follow-up after clear: 'Clear of conflict, returning to [assigned level], [callsign].'
Squawk 7600 immediately. Listen out on the last assigned frequency and on emergency guard (121.5).

Transmit blind on the last assigned frequency: '[Callsign], transmitting blind due to comms failure, squawking seven six zero zero, continuing flight planned route, descending to [level], estimating [waypoint] at [time].'
Keep transmitting blind at regular intervals stating intentions — receiver may be unreceived but ATC will sequence other traffic around your stated track and ETA.
Saying 'MAYDAY' only once. The three-time repetition is what makes it a recognised distress call — saying it once may be missed in frequency noise.
Confusing PAN-PAN with MAYDAY. PAN-PAN = urgency (priority handling); MAYDAY = distress (immediate threat). When in doubt and time is short, escalate to MAYDAY.
Describing the TCAS manoeuvre. 'TCAS RA' is the entire call. ATC knows what to do.
Not squawking 7600 on lost comms. The squawk is what tells ATC you're NORDO before any blind transmission gets through.
Not stating souls on board / fuel on MAYDAY/PAN-PAN. They are recommended (not strictly required), but SAR and ATC use them for diversion planning.

Cruise FL210 with Brisbane Centre. Left engine oil pressure drops to zero, no fire. Assessable, divertible — this is urgency, not distress. 'PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, Brisbane Centre, Mike X-ray Golf, oil pressure failure left engine, requesting descent and diversion to Coffs Harbour, four souls on board, two hours fuel.' Centre clears the airspace, you divert. Once on the ground at Coffs, cancel: 'Brisbane Centre, Mike X-ray Golf, cancel PAN PAN, situation resolved.'
